description:
We are a motivated 2-member team passionate about problem-solving, space data, and technology. We are participating in this year's NASA Space Apps Challenge to build an innovative solution using NASA's open-source data. 

We have skills in research, presentation, and design, and we are excited to work together, learn, and deliver a compelling project!
summary: CrewCompass is an offline-first crew health copilot for long space missions. On a Mars mission a message to Earth takes up to 22 minutes each way, so astronauts must spot their own health problems, and cabin air can cause symptoms that are hard to trace to a cause. Each day an astronaut completes a 60-second CrewCheck: symptom sliders, a mood question and a short reaction test. CrewCompass compares each astronaut with their own rolling baseline, tracks cabin CO2 against NASA's 2.5 mmHg guidance and 3 mmHg limit, and tests lagged links between symptoms and cabin conditions with a shuffle test, so chance patterns are not reported as causes. It then suggests environment-first actions from an offline library, escalates serious signs to the crew medical officer, and builds a compact health digest for Earth. Individual astronaut records are not public, so the symptoms in the demo are simulated and labeled, and the analysis is checked against a planted signal.
details:
WHAT IT DOES CrewCompass links how each astronaut feels to what the spacecraft cabin is doing, then tells them what to do next. It follows the challenge's three verbs: gather health indicators, evaluate status, support informed action. HOW IT WORKS - Gather: a 60-second daily CrewCheck (sliders for headache, vision change, congestion, fatigue and sleep quality, a mood question, and a 30-second reaction test), plus cabin series (CO2, temperature, humidity, radiation dose rate). - Evaluate: each astronaut is compared with their own rolling baseline (median and median absolute deviation, robust z-score). A persistence rule means one bad night only raises a "watch"; an alert needs the change to persist. A lasting vision change goes straight to the crew medical officer. Cabin CO2 is averaged over 1 hour and 7 days and compared with NASA's 3 mmHg limit and 2.5 mmHg guidance (mmHg = ppm x 760 / 1,000,000). - Attribute: lagged cross-correlation (0 to 72 hours) between each symptom and each cabin series, with a block-shuffle test so that chance patterns are not reported as causes. Confidence is capped at "medium" because fluid shift, which NASA links to the same symptoms, is not measured. - Act: environment-first action cards from an offline library, each with an escalation rule, and a compact health digest for Earth that waits for the next link. BENEFITS AND IMPACT Most health monitors say that something is wrong. CrewCompass says why it may be happening and what to try first, without waiting for a reply from Earth. A crew of four is too small for population thresholds, so personal baselines matter. Everything works with no connection. NASA DATA CO2 limits, the 7-day guidance and the conversion come from NASA's CO2 technical brief (OCHMO-TB-004 Rev D) and NASA-STD-3001. The app loads CSV exports from NASA's OSDR Environmental Data Application and uses such series as a stand-in for a cabin sensor series. These tables describe Rodent Research experiment conditions, not crew-cabin air, and we say so in the app. WHAT IS SIMULATED Individual astronaut health records are not public, so crew symptoms in the demo are simulated and labeled "simulated". The simulator can plant a known CO2-to-headache link, so the analysis can be tested: on 20 simulated missions it found the planted link in about 85% of astronaut series and raised false alarms in about 4% of series when none was planted. The strength of the planted link is illustrative, not calibrated to NASA data. CrewCompass is decision support, not a medical device. TOOLS Python (Starlette, NumPy, pandas, SciPy), SQLite, and an installable web app in plain JavaScript with a service worker. A single-file browser version runs the same analysis with no server. USE OF AI We used Claude (Anthropic) for translation between Arabic and English, research assistance, checking information against sources, and writing the code. The team reviewed everything and is responsible for it.

Full walkthrough video (under 3 minutes): https://youtu.be/9jLVdwy83GQ

Development Note & Transparency: The initial software boilerplate and core statistical simulation framework were prepared prior to the event as foundational tooling. During the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 hackathon window, the project was tailored to the challenge requirements, integrated with NASA OSDR environmental datasets and OCHMO-TB-004 thresholds, and finalized with the offline standalone build and documentation.
